hero.subtitle: Whether you were injured on a ranch, at a job site off Rt 150, or delivering along Ojai Avenue, a workplace injury can leave you unsure who's responsible. LawProactive connects you, free of charge, with an independent attorney who can sort through your options.

about.title: Ojai Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Ojai's economy leans on agriculture, hospitality, and small trades, and each of those jobs carries its own physical risks — from equipment accidents on orchards near Cuyama Road to slip-and-fall injuries at inns and restaurants along Ojai Avenue. When an on-the-job injury happens, California generally routes the claim through workers' compensation, which pays medical care and partial wages regardless of fault but usually blocks a lawsuit against your employer. That's not always the end of the story, though. If a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to what happened, you may have a separate claim against that third party. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect injured workers in Ojai with an independent attorney, free of charge, who can look at both the workers' comp side and any possible third-party angle so nothing gets missed.
about.ctaText: Talk to an independent attorney about your workplace injury, free of charge.

items.title: Two Paths Get Reviewed
items.desc: California law usually makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party can still open a separate claim. An attorney can check whether your case fits one path, both, or neither.

items.title: Deadlines Vary by Claim Type
items.desc: Reporting a workplace injury to your employer is generally due within 30 days, while a third-party injury claim carries its own 2-year filing deadline. Missing either window can limit your options, so timing matters.

items.title: Retaliation Protections Apply
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report an on-the-job injury. An independent attorney can help you understand those protections if you're worried about your job.

items.question: I was hurt working on a property in Ojai, not driving for my job. Does workers' comp still apply?
items.answer: In most cases, yes — workers' compensation generally covers injuries that happen while performing your job duties, whether that's on a ranch, at a job site, or in a shop along Grand Avenue. If a property owner or equipment maker outside your employer also contributed to the accident, that could open a separate third-party claim. An independent attorney can look at the specifics of where and how the injury happened.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly after a workplace injury?
items.answer: Generally no — California workers' compensation is typically the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault, which means a lawsuit against them is usually not an option. However, if someone other than your employer, like a subcontractor or equipment manufacturer, contributed to your injury, you may be able to pursue a separate claim against that party. An attorney can help sort out who may be responsible.

items.question: What if my employer discourages me from reporting my injury?
items.answer: Retaliation against an employee for reporting a workplace injury is illegal under California law. You generally have 30 days to report the injury to your employer, so acting promptly protects your rights. If you feel pressured not to report, an independent attorney connected through LawProactive can help you understand what protections apply.
